subject: Mathematics
title: Real Numbers
learningOutcomes: Explain, with examples, how civilizations (Sumerians, Egyptians, Romans, Indians, Arabs and the modern era) developed the number system.
Describe the real numbers as the union of rational and irrational numbers, \(\mathbb{R}=\mathbb{Q}\cup\mathbb{Q}^{\prime}\), using decimal forms and the number line.
Convert recurring decimals into \(\frac{p}{q}\) and find rational numbers between two given numbers.
Name, demonstrate and verify the additive, multiplicative, distributive, equality and order properties of real numbers.
Apply the laws of indices and radicals to simplify expressions, and rationalize the denominator using conjugate surds.
Apply real numbers to daily life: temperature conversions, profit and loss, profit sharing in a ratio and simple profit.

sections.heading: History of numbers
sections.body: The Sumerians used a base 60 (sexagesimal) system and the Egyptians a decimal (base 10) system. The Romans used seven letters I, V, X, L, C, D, M. The Indians developed the concept of zero and the decimal system (Indo-Arabic numerals), which Arab merchants carried to the West; al-Khwārizmī introduced algebra in the 9th century. The modern era added binary (base 2) and hexadecimal (base 16).

sections.heading: Rational and irrational numbers
sections.body: A rational number can be written as \(\frac{p}{q}\) with integers \(p,q\) and \(q\ne0\); its decimal form either terminates or is non-terminating and recurring. An irrational number has a non-terminating and non-recurring decimal form (for example \(\pi\), \(e\), \(\sqrt{2}\)). The real numbers are \(\mathbb{R}=\mathbb{Q}\cup\mathbb{Q}^{\prime}\). Rational + irrational is irrational, and non-zero rational × irrational is irrational.

sections.heading: Recurring decimals and the number line
sections.body: To convert a recurring decimal into \(\frac{p}{q}\), let \(x\) be the decimal, multiply by 10 (one repeating digit) or 100 (two repeating digits), and subtract. A rational number between two numbers is their average. A surd such as \(\sqrt{5}\) is located using a right-angled triangle (legs 2 and 1) and an arc, since \(2^2+1^2=5\).

sections.heading: Properties of real numbers
sections.body: Addition and multiplication have closure, commutative, associative, identity (0 and 1) and inverse properties (0 has no multiplicative inverse). Multiplication is distributive over addition and subtraction. Equality has reflexive, symmetric, transitive, additive, multiplicative and two cancellation properties. Order has trichotomy, transitive, additive, multiplicative, division and reciprocal properties; multiplying or dividing by a negative number reverses the inequality sign.

sections.heading: Radicals, indices and surds
sections.body: \(\sqrt[n]{a}=a^{1/n}\) where \(n\) is the index and \(a\) the radicand. Laws of indices: \(a^m a^n=a^{m+n}\), \((a^m)^n=a^{mn}\), \((ab)^n=a^nb^n\), \(\frac{a^m}{a^n}=a^{m-n}\), \(a^0=1\). A surd is an irrational radical with a rational radicand. Conjugate surds \(\sqrt{a}+\sqrt{b}\) and \(\sqrt{a}-\sqrt{b}\) multiply to the rational number \(a-b\), which is used to rationalize denominators.

sections.heading: Real numbers in daily life
sections.body: Temperature: \(K={}^{\circ}C+273\), \({}^{\circ}C=\frac{5}{9}({}^{\circ}F-32)\), \({}^{\circ}F=\frac{9}{5}{}^{\circ}C+32\). Profit = SP − CP, Loss = CP − SP, and the percentage is taken on CP. A profit is shared in a ratio by dividing it in proportion to the ratio parts. Rate of simple profit \(=\frac{\text{profit}\times100}{\text{time}\times\text{principal}}\).

definitions.definition: A number of the form \(\frac{p}{q}\), \(p,q\in\mathbb{Z}\), \(q\ne0\); its decimal form terminates or is non-terminating and recurring.
A number that cannot be written as a quotient of integers; its decimal form is non-terminating and non-recurring.
The union of the rational and irrational numbers, \(\mathbb{R}=\mathbb{Q}\cup\mathbb{Q}^{\prime}\).
In \(\sqrt[n]{a}\), \(a\) is the radicand and \(n\) is the index of the radical.
An irrational radical with a rational radicand, such as \(\sqrt{5}\) or \(\sqrt[3]{11}\); \(\sqrt{9}\) and \(\sqrt{\pi}\) are not surds.
Multiplying the numerator and denominator by the conjugate to remove surds from the denominator.
For real numbers \(a,b\), exactly one of \(a<b\), \(a=b\), \(a>b\) holds.

examTips: For a recurring decimal, multiply by 10 when one digit repeats and by 100 when two digits repeat, then subtract and reduce the fraction.
Multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative number reverses the sign; check the sign of the multiplier first.
To rationalize \(\frac{k}{\sqrt{a}\pm\sqrt{b}}\), multiply by the conjugate and use \((\sqrt{a})^2-(\sqrt{b})^2=a-b\) for the new denominator.
A negative index means a reciprocal: \(a^{-n}=\frac{1}{a^n}\); write the base as a power first when the index is a fraction.
Percentage profit and loss are always calculated on the cost price, not the selling price.
